#2709. 49ers trade deadline grade reveals winners and losers from deals

All teams serious about making a Super Bowl run made sure to take advantage of the trade deadline, and the San Francisco 49ers addressed their concerns.

The 49ers have a 7-1 record through Week 9 without a fully healthy roster. All throughout the season, they've missed multiple starters and key players. The most impacted positions were defensive line and wide receiver.

There was a clear focus at the trade deadline and the Niners addressed it in two separate trades with the Indianapolis Colts, bringing former 49ers defensive lineman DeForest Buckner and ex-Cal wide receiver Keenan Allen back to the Bay Area.

San Francisco faced a number of injuries to their receiving core: Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel Sr., De'Zhaun Stribling, Ricky Pearsall and Christian Kirk. The good news for the 49ers is Samuel trending in the right direction. Niners head coach Kyle Shanahan told reporters Monday that he expects to have Samuel back at practice on Wednesday.

Injuries also plagued a number of defensive linemen, including rookie Gracen Halton, who dislocated his ankle in a Nov. 8 win against the Las Vegas Raiders. He was placed on IR, the team announced Tuesday.

Other injuries on the D-line included Nick Bosa, Mykel Williams, Alfred Collins, Sam Okuayinonu, CJ West, Mikail Kamara and Andrew Farmer II. Bosa returned against the Raiders after missing time with a knee and calf injury. Shanahan said he also expects West back at practice.

Allen and Buckner come in as immediate plug-ins to help solve San Francisco's health issues as the team as players look to make their eventual return to the gridiron.

The 49ers earn an overall trade grade of a "B" for their moves.

NFL trade grades: NFL trade deadline grades reveal which team won every major deal

The 49ers made only two moves, same team, different days. Their first trade was for Buckner on Oct. 27, then moments before the trade deadline, the circled back to the Colts and dealt for Allen.

The 49ers' trade return has been to their benefit early on. Defensively, San Francisco wanted to get into the backfield more often, fill gaps and pressure quarterbacks. Although only two trades were made, the Niners still made it worth their while.

Bringing back Buckner from the Colts added to the defense's continuity led by Fred Warner, Dre Greenlaw and Bosa. Buckner's presence had an immediate impact in his first game was against the Raiders, although he didn't register a sack and had just one tackle.

"I thought we hit the quarterback a lot. I thought we also rushed really well in some key situations," Shanahan said on Monday. "Buckner got him on the ground a number of times. [DL] Keion [White] got him on the ground a couple times. [Las Vegas Raiders QB] Kirk's [Cousins] pretty good at getting rid of the ball when we do beat someone, but I thought our pass rush and the pressure on the quarterback, I thought we had a good game in that manner."

Allen was brought back to California. He started his NFL career in 2013 with the then-San Diego Chargers, spending the first 10 years of his NFL career with that team and earning six Pro Bowl selections. Allen made a name for himself as a possession receiver who was an exquisite in route runner.

He's added to a wide receiver room that will eventually get back Evans and Samuel. Scary.

The 49ers have been hanging on with the healthy receivers they have such as Jordan Watkins, Demarcus Robinson, Jacob Cowing and recently signed vet Brandin Cooks. They've been holding it down while their stars get back.

"I think [Cooks] has been effective. I think we went to him twice yesterday and [QB] Brock [Purdy] got to him twice and made both of those plays. He's been doing like everyone else," Shanahan said. "I think he doesn't have many busts. I think he's getting used to the offense and being a part of the group and I think all those guys have, there's not really one guy ahead of the other too much."

While Purdy has missed his much-anticipated target in Evans, it's created more anonymity in the 49ers offense.

"You never know where the ball is going to go," Shanahan said. "I think Jordan Watkins has been playing real well and he got more opportunities yesterday. His touchdown pass, he was fourth in the progression on that play. Brock went all the way across the board and got it to him and he made the play. There were other plays he was first in the progression and it's no different for Brandin Cooks and any of the other guys.

"It was no different for [WR Demarcus Robinson] D-Rob in the game," he added. "But I've been real happy with Brandin and how he's been blocking. When the ball's come his way, I think he's done a good job making the plays for the most part."

A week ago when looking at potential trade targets for the 49ers, a heavy suggestion was to revisit the Colts, since they already made a deal for Buckner, and ask for another player. This time a wide receiver.

The 49ers did that, but they didn't get the expected guy. No shade whatsoever to Allen, because it's still a great pickup. However, a 25-year-old slot receiver in Josh Downs went to the Kansas City Chiefs. Featuring similar stats to Allen, Downs piled up 33 receptions for 354 yards and a touchdown through nine games. He averaged 10.7 yards per catch.

When it's all said and done, the Niners still have Brandon Aiyuk following his reinstatement by the NFL. San Francisco was given an additional two weeks to determine how they would proceed with his contract, whether to trade, keep or release Aiyuk. The Niners' two-week exemption ends on Nov. 23.

The trade deadline passed. So, there goes that idea. The 49ers could keep Aiyuk, if they wanted to use him still.

Shanahan has more than blatantly indicated that he does not expect Aiyuk to be a part of the team. Therefore, the next option would be to release him.

Aiyuk's agent Drew Rosenhaus said on "The Pat McAfee Show" that he expects Aiyuk to compete on some team upon his eventual release from the 49ers.

"Brandon will either play for the 49ers when the two weeks is up, or they can decide to release him, by which he will be a free agent, and I expect that there will be interest in him," Rosenhaus said. "I definitely expect him to play this season. Judging the comments from coach Shanahan, it doesn't sound like they plan on bringing Brandon back."

#2707. CBA allows 49ers to not pay Brandon Aiyuk during two-week roster exemption

When unusual situations emerge in the NFL, it becomes a piece-by-piece exercise in figuring out the specific rules that apply. And few situations have been more unusual than 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk’s odyssey of the past year.

He’s back on the 49ers, at a salary of $13.75 million for the rest of the season. That fact pointed to the 49ers releasing him by 4:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, in order to avoid owing him one-ninth of the total amount ($1.52 million) for Week 10.

But here’s where yet another obscure wrinkle applies. Under Article 20, Section 4 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement, the 49ers owe Aiyuk nothing during his two-week roster exemption.

From the relevant provision: “If a Club obtains a roster exemption for a player under contract who does not report to his Club at least five days before the final day of Preseason Training Camp as defined in Article 23, Section 10, the player will not be entitled to preseason or regular season compensation until such exemption is removed, provided the player is given written notice of such fact upon reporting to the Club. If such notice is not given to the player, the player must be paid his Paragraph 5 Salary during his exemption.”

So if the 49ers gave Aiyuk written notice that he won’t be paid during the two-week roster exemption (and they surely did), they don’t have to pay him. Which pushes their deadline for avoiding owing him a game check until Tuesday, November 24 — one day after the expiration of the exemption.

Why not just cut him? The 49ers are delaying the move because they can, postponing by up to two weeks his passage through waivers and, given his salary, inevitable free agency.

In the interim, he’s on the team. But Aiyuk won’t be reporting for work on Wednesday. He has been excused, we’re told, from team activities and he’s working out on his own.

The 49ers could release him at any moment. There’s no reason not to do so, other than to apply the brakes to his ability to join another team.

The circumstances counter the notion that he was reinstated by the league subject to any type of agreement with the 49ers. If that had happened, the agreement surely would have included a requirement that the 49ers promptly cut him.

Which means that the NFL, after apparently working with the 49ers to delay Aiyuk’s reinstatement in order to help the 49ers recover bonus money from Aiyuk, finally decided that reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list can’t be delayed in order to advance a team’s strategic objectives.

So, yes, Aiyuk eventually will be released. He wasn’t released today because the 49ers don’t owe him a game check for Week 10, or for Week 11. Eventually, when the roster exemption expires, they’ll cut him.

For now, the team’s delay in doing the inevitable points to a desire to keep another team from getting him, sticking it to Aiyuk, or some of both. It’s petty, but the 49ers have the power to do it.

#2703. Lakers waive Lawson Lovering, sign Carson Cooper

The Lakers are continuing to make moves on the margin while trying to find a potential center solution. After signing Lawson Lovering to a two-way deal roughly two weeks ago, the Lakers are waiving the big man in place of…another big man.

Carson Cooper, a 6'10" center, will take Lovering's place on a two-way deal, all according to Michael Scotto of HoopsHype.

Cooper appeared in one game with the Grizzlies this year, playing for just three minutes. He signed a two-way deal with Memphis after going undrafted in the 2026 NBA Draft.

At Michigan State, Cooper averaged 11.1 points and 7.1 rebounds while shooting 58.4% from the field. He only averaged one block per game and attempted five threes all season.

Lovering only had some brief cameos with the Lakers, all coming in garbage time, during his stint with the Lakers. He was with the parent team at the start of the G League season, so he did not play with Coachella Valley.

Given how the Lakers are currently playing and how little real NBA experience he has, it's unlikely to expect much from Cooper. The team is shuffling through options, but none of them appear all that intriguing on paper. For now, these are all makeshift, break-in-case-of-emergency solutions that likely won't play.

The action will stream exclusively for members at live.onefc.com.

Meanwhile, Rodtang begins his own tournament journey against fellow Thai legend Nong-O Hama at The Inner Circle 38 on November 13. The quarterfinal winner will advance to face either Shimon Yoshinari or Ramadan Ondash in the semifinals.

That creates the possibility of an extraordinary final between two generations of flyweight Muay Thai greatness. And although Imangazaliev welcomes that possibility, he knows the star-studded bracket offers no guarantees.

"Yes, it would be very nice for me if Rodtang makes it. I want to fight Rodtang after Aslamjon. But things have changed a little bit, and I don't know now.

"It doesn't matter. If I need to fight someone else, no problem. But [Ramadan] Ondash and Shimon are also a very good fight, two younger guys in this Grand Prix. Too much action, you know."

A potential meeting would carry immense significance for both men. Rodtang ruled the division for five years and became a global sensation through his relentless aggression, durability, and electrifying performances.

Imangazaliev, meanwhile, has established himself as the division's new standard-bearer, defeating Kongthoranee Sor Sommai, Nong-O, and Ortikov during his unbeaten rise to World Title glory.

The Dagestani recognizes Rodtang's legendary status, though he admits he cannot judge his potential rival's current motivation from the outside. In his view, achieving enormous success can present athletes with a different kind of challenge.

"You know, when you have too much money, when you have everything, maybe you can get tired of the sport, of the discipline. You need to make weight. You need to train two times a day, every day.

"But when you have everything, maybe when you wake up in the morning, you think, 'I have everything. Why do I need this?' And maybe he's not hungry. But I don't know. Maybe he's still hungry too. But for me, it doesn't matter, you know, because I'm hungry. I know inside I have fire. I'm ready."

That hunger has fueled Imangazaliev's remarkable ascent through ONE, where he has combined spectacular finishes with the confidence to challenge established names regardless of their reputations.

Yet the reigning king has little interest in lengthy comparisons with his fellow contenders. Rather than declare himself superior in every department, he prefers to let his performances demonstrate the qualities that separate him from the competition.

"I don't need to speak about this because people can see it in my fights. My technique is different, my mind, my mentality, my character, everything is different.

"Every fighter is different, of course, but I'm here to stay champion."

For reigning ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Champion Asadula Imangazaliev, the prospect of facing Rodtang is only one attraction in an eight-man tournament featuring some of the finest Muay Thai talent from around the world.

With the prestigious silver Grand Prix belt and ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Title at stake, the competition brings together established legends, dangerous contenders, and young phenoms capable of changing the division's landscape.

Imangazaliev expects every quarterfinal to deliver a demanding test. Even as the reigning king, he sees a field packed with opponents who have earned their opportunity to compete for the sport's biggest prizes.

"Every fight is tough. But I think there will be very, very good fights in this Grand Prix.

"First, my fight with Aslamjon. But of course, there are legends also, Rodtang and Nong-O, and all the younger fighters."

On Imangazaliev's side of the bracket, the winner of Black Panther versus Ubaid Hussain could stand between him and a place in the final.

The tournament's format also means that his rematch with Ortikov comes immediately, rather than later in the competition. But for the Dagestani, the bracket's arrangement changes nothing about the opportunity before him.

"I think [me and Ortikov] could also be a very good final, but if we fight first, no problem. For me, it doesn't matter. I came here only to take everything.

"It doesn't matter to me who my opponent is, who is first or second. I just came to take the belt."

#2701. Apparently, kicking Devin Booker in the nuts is a judgment call

If there's one thing that gets my blood boiling and sends me rushing to my keyboard, furiously typing away while using this space as a personal therapy session, it's NBA officiating. And once again, we witnessed not only inconsistency during last night's matchup between the Phoenix Suns and San Antonio Spurs, but inconsistency in how the league ultimately assessed the consequences.

Let me set the stage for you. It's the third quarter, and the Suns are trailing by 20 points. Keldon Johnson grabs an offensive rebound and goes up for a shot from about three feet away. In the process, he kicks his leg out, making forceful contact with Devin Booker's junk. That's right. Right in the family jewels.

Booker immediately collapses to the floor, writhing in pain, and the officials? Play on. Nothing to see here. Apparently, a man getting kicked squarely in the equipment isn't enough to warrant a second look, let alone a review for a potential flagrant foul.

Now, when you watch the replay, you can make the argument that Johnson's leg movement was part of his natural shooting motion. Perhaps he was extending his leg to maintain balance while attempting the shot. I'll entertain that explanation because we witnessed something remarkably similar last week when Dillon Brooks attempted a jump shot with Jamal Murray defending him.

Did it appear that Brooks extended his leg a little farther than necessary? Absolutely. But anyone who watches Brooks regularly knows that he frequently kicks his leg out when shooting. It's part of how he stabilizes himself in the air. Perhaps it's also a technique designed to draw contact, but it's hardly an unusual movement for him.

Regardless, Brooks was assessed a Flagrant 2 foul and ejected from the game. Meanwhile, against a San Antonio Spurs franchise with a long and storied history of kicking the Suns in the nuts, Johnson wasn't even assessed a common foul. There's your first inconsistency.

Then, today, the NBA reviewed the incident and retroactively assessed Johnson a Flagrant 1 foul. So apparently, what wasn't even worthy of a whistle during the game was serious enough to warrant a flagrant penalty after the fact. Wonderful. Thanks for clearing that up.

We've been down this road before. The league acknowledges an officiating mistake after the game, but that acknowledgment does absolutely nothing for the team that was denied the call in real time. Granted, Phoenix was trailing by 20 points when the incident occurred. I'm certainly not suggesting that a whistle would have changed the outcome of the game.

But that's not the point. The point is consistency.

Johnson receives a retroactive Flagrant 1, while Brooks was assessed a Flagrant 2 and immediately ejected for a play that, when you compare the footage, appears remarkably similar. So what exactly separates the two incidents? Was Brooks being assessed a reputation tax? Is his history as a physical, occasionally antagonistic defender influencing how officials interpret his actions? Or are we witnessing another example of inconsistent officiating from referees whose judgment deserves scrutiny?

Because I'm beginning to wonder whether there's a bias at play when he officiates Suns games. Much like Tyler Ford, the official who ejected Brooks, Van Duyne has developed a history of calls involving Phoenix that have left me questioning his judgment. The officiating statistics surrounding both referees only add to that frustration, particularly when examining how frequently they've whistled the Suns for fouls.

And these two have history together. Remember when Devin Booker was ejected during a nationally televised matchup against the Los Angeles Lakers a few years ago? Ford and Van Duyne were both involved in the sequence that resulted in Booker receiving technical fouls and being tossed from the game. It's one of those moments that remains lodged in my basketball memory, and incidents like last night's do little to improve my confidence in the officiating.

This is the kind of stuff that really ticks my bombs. If the NBA wants to hold players accountable for excessive or dangerous contact, I'm all for it. Protect the players. Enforce the rules. Assess flagrant fouls when the situation warrants them. But for the love of God, establish some consistency in how those rules are applied.

While we're at it, how about a little accountability for the officials themselves? If the league can review a play the following day and determine that Johnson committed a Flagrant 1 foul, shouldn't there be some acknowledgment that the officiating crew, including Van Duyne, failed to recognize it when it actually mattered?

Because retroactively assigning a penalty might correct the league's paperwork, but it does absolutely nothing to correct what happened on the basketball court. And until there's greater consistency and accountability, I'll continue finding myself right here, furiously typing away, wondering how the same league can look at two remarkably similar plays and somehow arrive at three different conclusions.

#2700. In Kirk Cousins, the Vikings landed their first choice

After last night's abysmal performance by the offense against the Bills, the Vikings mobilized to trade for a quarterback. Ultimately, they got the guy they wanted.

Per a source with knowledge of the situation, Kirk Cousins was Minnesota's first choice.

The Vikings explored other options. Multiple players, including fellow former Vikings quarterback Daniel Jones.

Cousins's history with the team makes it easier to get him up to speed. He had 25 regular-season games with coach Kevin O'Connell, and four seasons with receiver Justin Jefferson.

The existence of options may have helped the Vikings keep the compensation to only a third-round pick. Given the level of desperation, the Vikings seemed destined to give up more than that to fix a problem that threatened to implode the season.

That's not an overstatement. The dam was breaking. Frustration was rampant during the debacle against the Bills, on both sides of the ball.

It was a simple proposition. If the Vikings didn't trade for a quarterback on Tuesday, they could not be considered a serious franchise.

In the end, they managed to stop the bleeding by sending their third-round pick (their own, not the one they acquired from the Eagles for defensive end Jonathan Greenard) to the Raiders for Cousins.

It's unclear how much better things will be with Cousins back in the fold. It can't get worse than what they put on the field for Week 9.

#2698. Luka Doncic points to key area Lakers can vastly improve to bolster championship odds

The Lakers have the NBA's best record at 10-2. They've won six games in a row. They have the highest-rated offense (121.5). They're considered real championship contenders.

Luka Doncic #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers plays defense against the Atlanta Hawks during a game in Atlanta, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

They're rated 19th defensively. Lakers superstar Luka Doncic believes they can claw their way up those rankings.

"I think we can be [good defensively], but honestly I think we just kind of relax a little bit a couple minutes in the game," Doncic said after the Lakers' 124-114 win over the Hawks on Monday. "So that allows the team [to] make the run. I think we just gotta figure that out. I think we can be way better than [19th]. I think we have the potential for that."

Doncic, who has been dragged through the mud throughout his career for his defense, has made marked improvements in that area this season, including finishing with 32 points, eight rebounds, 10 assists, five steals and two blocked shots against the Hawks.

Doncic, who leads the league in scoring at 39.3 points per game and is having an MVP-caliber start to the season, has shown much more effort on the less glamorous side of the court through his first 10 games.

Atlanta Hawks forward Onyeka Okongwu (17) vies for a rebound against Los Angeles Lakers center Walker Kessler (14) on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, in Atlanta. AP Photo/Mike Stewart

He leads the NBA in defensive loose balls recovered (nine) and is tied for second in charges drawn (four).

As a team, the Lakers really falter defensively when Walker Kessler is off the court. And they're tied for second-to-last in the league in rebounding with 40.3 per game.

Atlanta Hawks guard Nickeil Alexander-Walker (7) shoots against Los Angeles Lakers forward Ziaire Williams (11) on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Atlanta. AP Photo/Mike Stewart

But they're showing a lot of signs that they're putting in the effort to become a good defensive team.

The Lakers rank second in the NBA in steals per game (10.8), second in total deflections (240) and third in blocks per game (6.4).

Kessler, their defensive anchor, leads the league in contested shots (140), and Matisse Thybulle is second in deflections (50).

#2693. Fantasy Football Panic Meter: Matthew Stafford heads to Coping Corner after Puka Nacua injury

At this point in the season, we have to adjust our expectations. Some of these players still belong in your fantasy football lineup, but that doesn't mean you should feel good about them. The categories remain No Panic, Some Panic, Total Panic and Coping Corner. Nobody here gets No Panic from me.

With Jonathan Taylor staying in Indianapolis, I have total panic. Total panic.

Over the last two games, Taylor has combined for 21 carries, 69 rushing yards and no touchdowns. With two lost fumbles, he's averaged 5.8 half-PPR points. His carries dropped from 21 and 18 in Weeks 6 and 7 to 8 and 13 in Weeks 8 and 9.

He was productive in those earlier games. This hasn't been a month of nothing. But the direction should concern everybody who rosters Taylor.

I've been watching Taylor's usage and wondering whether the Colts were holding him back in case they traded him. I don't know that. I do know I want him out of there.

I don't trust this offense with Daniel Jones. Indianapolis traded Quenton Nelson, its All-Pro guard and, in everyone's opinion, its best offensive lineman.

Taylor is a running back who can catch passes. He is not a pass-catching weapon who plays running back. His nine catches over the last two games produced 42 yards. That hasn't come close to rescuing him from bad rushing days.

And I expect the Colts to spend plenty of time trailing. That's a problem when the passing game isn't giving the team's best offensive player much help, especially after Indianapolis traded two of its top receivers, Josh Downs and Keenan Allen, on Tuesday.

I would have loved a move that gave Taylor a chance to thrive. Instead, he's banished to this offense, and we should be very, very concerned.

Every week, there's another reason to believe the Chase Brown game is coming. The receiving work. The offense. The matchup. Then we're disappointed again.

Brown hasn't scored a rushing touchdown since Week 1. That's seven games and 87 carries. He hasn't scored a receiving touchdown or reached 100 rushing yards in a game this season either. He's averaged 8.6 half-PPR points over his last four appearances. Cincinnati scored at least 31 points in all four. This offense is producing. Brown just isn't getting enough of the fantasy payoff.

Joe Burrow is playing at an MVP level with 23 passing touchdowns. The Bengals have five rushing touchdowns as a team. This offense runs through Burrow. Brown can help with dump-offs when Cincinnati is chasing points, but those receiving spikes are hard to predict. He caught eight passes in Week 8 and three the following week.

I've got Some Panic because I know what I'm getting: a volatile mid-to-low-end RB2 with sporadic receiving upside. I'm done treating every week like the breakout is right around the corner.

I talked about this on the Yahoo Data Dump show. I've been concerned about Derrick Henry.

The crown has fallen. He is no longer the king.

Henry is 32, and Father Time always wins. Give him a runway and he can still get north and south quickly. But I'm not seeing him make defenders miss the way this offense needs him to, and I think this offensive line has been dreadful. The season totals look fine until you're actually living with these afternoons.

Seven of his eight rushing touchdowns came in the first four weeks. Over his last four games, Henry has 62 carries for 213 yards and one rushing touchdown. That's 3.4 yards per carry. He's added four catches for 13 yards.

Baltimore scored 10, 13, 10 and 10 points in those games. Its last three losses were all by at least 20 points. The defense isn't keeping games close, and the offense isn't creating enough scoring opportunities.

Could Jacoby Brissett help? Sure. Jesse Minter says Brissett is going to start in Week 10. But I need to see it. Brissett doesn't immediately fix the blocking, the defense or my concerns about Henry himself. Total Panic. You're playing him as a mid-to-low-end RB2 right now.

The only reason Jayden Daniels isn't in Total Panic is that my expectations have been adjusted. I hope yours have, too. He returned from the elbow injury in Week 5 and ran for 103 yards and two touchdowns. The rushing alone gave you 22.3 fantasy points.

Since then, he has 10 carries for 49 yards and no rushing touchdowns across three games. That's about 1.6 fantasy points per game from rushing.

The passing hasn't completely fallen apart. Daniels threw for 300 yards and two touchdowns in Week 6. But his last two fantasy scores were 14.98 and 14.56. Without the rushing advantage, there's much less room for an ordinary passing performance.

Terry McLaurin is out for the season, and Washington doesn't have many pass-catching options to replace him. The margin for success is smaller.

I've got Some Panic because I'm no longer expecting Daniels to automatically give me the advantage I drafted him for. If there's a better weekly streaming option, I'm considering it. He's no longer a must-play quarterback for me.

I have total, total panic about this situation. Matthew Stafford belongs in Coping Corner. He wasn't giving us enough with Puka Nacua. Now, Puka is likely headed to injured reserve with MCL and PCL sprains along with turf toe. Stafford has averaged 200.5 passing yards and 13.47 fantasy points over his last four games. He hasn't reached 250 passing yards in any of them. His last two fantasy scores were 8.28 and 11.22.

We were already talking ourselves into starting him. Now, we're taking away his best receiving option. Head coach Sean McVay expects Davante Adams back toward the shorter end of his 6-10 week window. But what does "sooner" mean for your lineup right now?

Stafford is 38, and to me, he's showing his age. His right elbow was on the Week 9 injury report, although he practiced fully. I can't tell you the elbow explains everything, but this situation gives me little confidence.

With Puka, Stafford was streamable. Without Puka and Davante, he's a quarterback I have zero interest in starting.

Drake London is in Total Panic, too. Michael Penix Jr. has not been good. This offense has not been good. London is still Atlanta's leading receiver, but that doesn't make me feel better about the situation.

Over his last four games, London has 17 catches for 204 yards and one touchdown, averaging 8.7 half-PPR points. Over the last two, he has six catches for 76 yards and no touchdowns.

Penix has combined for 287 passing yards, one touchdown and five interceptions across those two games. How much confidence are we supposed to have in London delivering WR1 production in that environment? London has 692 receiving yards this season, so there have been productive games. But he has one receiving touchdown, and this recent connection hasn't been good enough.

You drafted him in the first round to be your WR1. This isn't close to what you needed.

I have low faith in Penix right now, and that directly affects how I feel about London.

The talent hasn't changed. My confidence in this offense consistently getting that talent into your fantasy lineup has. I'm not comfortable pretending the situation is fine.

#2690. Justin Herbert, Khalil Mack remain with Chargers after trade deadline

The Los Angeles Chargers had an opportunity to be true sellers after a 0-8 start to the season, only to land somewhere closer to the middle.

Coach Jim Harbaugh and the Chargers haven't found much success during the 2026 NFL season, but there remains this sense of belief in each other.

That was on display again Tuesday with the decision to keep potential trade assets – such as quarterback Justin Herbert and outside linebacker Khalil Mack – on the roster.

The Chargers finished both the 2024 and 2025 seasons at 11-6, raising expectations that the team would be back in the playoff mix. Both of those players were around during that successful run and remain with the franchise to help make something out of the current season.

While expectations of a playoff appearance have nearly evaporated, here's why the Chargers likely decided to stay with their stars.

More: Winless Chargers make first move of NFL trade deadline with AFC West partner

Herbert could've been an attractive trade target for a few teams across the league, but a down season has tanked his stock and put him at the center of the Chargers' struggles.

Herbert has completed 144 of 235 (61.5%) of his passes for 1,591 yards, six touchdowns and 11 interceptions this season. He's also been sacked 31 times. Herbert suffering a finger injury in the same game he was sacked eight times this past weekend didn't help his stock much either.

Herbert's current contract would keep him with the Chargers through the 2029 season and includes a no-trade clause, according to Spotrac. If the team were serious about trading the quarterback, Herbert would've had a say in any potential destinations.

More: Chargers fail to make big moves at trade deadline despite abysmal season

Mack was likely the Chargers' best trade asset, but he remains in Los Angeles.

Both Mack and coach Jim Harbaugh stated publicly that the outside linebacker wanted to remain with the Chargers, despite the lost season. Mack signed a one-year deal during the offseason to remain with LA. It is his third consecutive one-year deal with the Chargers.

While the coach has provided fairly vague answers regarding Herbert and the job security for his offensive coordinator, Mike McDaniel, Harbaugh provided a clear stance.

"I want Khalil Mack here," Harbaugh told reporters earlier this month. "Khalil Mack wants to be here. He's one of the pillars of our team."

Mack shared a similar sentiment regarding the trade rumors and his desire to remain a Charger.

"They know how I feel, man," Mack said via The Athletic. "It's just tough with all the outside noise. And so, ultimately, I want to be here and help them win.

"Even though it's tough right now, you always see the light at the end of the tunnel."

Mack has 22 total tackles, three sacks and five tackles for a loss this season.

#2688. NBA issues retroactive flagrant foul to Keldon Johnson after officials missed his blatant groin kick of Devin Booker

Keldon Johnson got away with shenanigans in real time. But the NBA's not letting him off the hook.

The NBA announced Tuesday that it's issued a postgame Flagrant Foul 1 to the San Antonio Spurs guard for an infraction during Monday's blowout win over the Phoenix Suns.

The infraction? He kicked Devin Booker in the groin, very clearly so. Booker went down to the court in obvious pain. But game officials chose to move along as if nothing happened.

Here's the incriminating video the Suns were happy to post on their social media Tuesday.

That isn't subtle. Referee Natalie Sago was standing with a clear view of the infraction, and nothing was called on the floor. So play ensued as Booker writhed in pain on the court until the Suns were forced to call a timeout.

But there was a chance to rectify the situation from there. Per the NBA rulebook, coaches aren't permitted to challenge a non-call. Suns coach Jordan Ott had no recourse to initiate a replay review.

But game officials do. Under the "Altercation" heading in the NBA rulebook, officials may initiate a replay review absent a foul called on the floor when:

A player, coach, trainer or other bench person commits a hostile act against another player, referee, coach, trainer, bench person or spectator

This is generally applied when there's a two-way altercation. If Booker had kicked Johnson in the groin in response, they would have almost certainly gone to the tape to issue Johnson his deserved flagrant foul that really warranted Flagrant 2 with an ejection.

But the language clearly gives officials leeway to go to the monitor when a player "commits a hostile act against another player." A groin kick is the definition of a hostile act. NBA referees are more than happy to stop play to go to the monitor for lesser infractions.

The only solace here is that the game was a blowout. The Spurs held a 15-point lead at the time in a game they won, 122-96. A properly called flagrant foul wasn't likely to shift the outcome of the game.

But that's likely of little comfort to Booker. Game officials need to do better.

#2686. CBA allows 49ers to not pay Brandon Aiyuk during two-week roster exemption

When unusual situations emerge in the NFL, it becomes a piece-by-piece exercise in figuring out the specific rules that apply. And few situations have been more unusual than 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk's odyssey of the past year.

He's back on the 49ers, at a salary of $13.75 million for the rest of the season. That fact pointed to the 49ers releasing him by 4:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, in order to avoid owing him one-ninth of the total amount ($1.52 million) for Week 10.

But here's where yet another obscure wrinkle applies. Under Article 20, Section 4 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement, the 49ers owe Aiyuk nothing during his two-week roster exemption.

From the relevant provision: "If a Club obtains a roster exemption for a player under contract who does not report to his Club at least five days before the final day of Preseason Training Camp as defined in Article 23, Section 10, the player will not be entitled to preseason or regular season compensation until such exemption is removed, provided the player is given written notice of such fact upon reporting to the Club. If such notice is not given to the player, the player must be paid his Paragraph 5 Salary during his exemption."

So if the 49ers gave Aiyuk written notice that he won't be paid during the two-week roster exemption (and they surely did), they don't have to pay him. Which pushes their deadline for avoiding owing him a game check until Tuesday, November 24 — one day after the expiration of the exemption.

Why not just cut him? The 49ers are delaying the move because they can, postponing by up to two weeks his passage through waivers and, given his salary, inevitable free agency.

In the interim, he's on the team. But Aiyuk won't be reporting for work on Wednesday. He has been excused, we're told, from team activities and he's working out on his own.

The 49ers could release him at any moment. There's no reason not to do so, other than to apply the brakes to his ability to join another team.

The circumstances counter the notion that he was reinstated by the league subject to any type of agreement with the 49ers. If that had happened, the agreement surely would have included a requirement that the 49ers promptly cut him.

Which means that the NFL, after apparently working with the 49ers to delay Aiyuk's reinstatement in order to help the 49ers recover bonus money from Aiyuk, finally decided that reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list can't be delayed in order to advance a team's strategic objectives.

So, yes, Aiyuk eventually will be released. He wasn't released today because the 49ers don't owe him a game check for Week 10, or for Week 11. Eventually, when the roster exemption expires, they'll cut him.

For now, the team's delay in doing the inevitable points to a desire to keep another team from getting him, sticking it to Aiyuk, or some of both. It's petty, but the 49ers have the power to do it.

#2683. Jayson Tatum responds to Jaylen Brown snub with runaway Celtics win over 76ers paced by Paul George's 36 points

Jaylen Brown delivered the opening message with a pregame snub Tuesday night. But it was Jayson Tatum, Paul George and the Boston Celtics who got the last word in a runaway 123-101 win over Brown's Philadelphia 76ers.

The game marked the anticipated first meeting between Tatum and Brown since their highly publicized split as Celtics teammates. The pair led Boston to an NBA championship, but are off to a bitter start as rivals after Brown's offseason trade to the 76ers.

Tatum got the best of Brown in the blowout win with 21 points, 6 rebounds, 4 assists and 2 blocks. Brown got into early foul trouble with three first-half fouls and struggled to get much of anything going. He finished with 13 points, 5 rebounds, 2 assists and 4 turnovers.

In the end, it was George who took on the starring role against his former team. George was part of the return from Philadelphia in the deal to acquire Brown from the Celtics. He caught fire and led all scorers with 36 points and five rebounds while shooting 14 of 22 from the field and 6 of 11 from 3.

The tension was on display from the opening tip as Brown openly snubbed Tatum in front of 20,000-plus fans in Philadelphia and a national TV audience. Brown said prior to Tuesday's highly anticipated 76ers-Celtics game that he didn't intend to speak with Tatum.

As players took the court before tipoff, Tatum approached his former Celtics teammate in an effort to dap Brown up. Brown, who was busy spinning the basketball, acted like Tatum didn't exist.

Tatum then moved on to Brown's teammate, LeBron James, who was happy to share some pregame love with his rival before getting down to the business of basketball.

It was awkward to say the least and left Tatum standing at midcourt next to Brown like a man who'd just been left hanging.

The ball was then mercifully tipped to break the pregame tension. After the game, Brown told reporters he was simply trying to focus rather than snub Tatum, via ESPN's Kris Rhim:

"I'm just focused on coming out and doing what's best for my team. Everything else was just — to be honest, I wasn't paying attention. But credit to Jayson, he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics, they executed, shot the hell out of the ball. They were the better team tonight."

When the game action started, it was Tatum who struck the first blow. In their first one-on-one matchup of the game, Brown sized Tatum up from the wing beyond the 3-point arc. Tatum smothered him and poked the ball away off Brown and out of bounds for a turnover.

Tatum went on to score 11 first-quarter points as the Celtics finished the frame with a 30-23 lead.

From there Tatum and Brown spent much of the game guarding each other when they shared the court. But Tatum made his biggest mark on the game with a poster dunk on James in the second half as the 76ers were closing the gap from a 13-point third-quarter deficit.

The 76ers did battle back to tie the game at 76. But hot Celtics 3-point shooting paced by George opened the game up down the stretch as Boston opened its lead to as much as 25 points.

The Celtics shot 50.5% from the field and 44.9% (22 of 45) from 3 while holding the 76ers to 41.8% shooting and a 29.7% clip (11 of 37) from 3.

Tyrese Maxey led the 76ers with 24 points. James tallied 11 points, 8 rebounds and 5 assists while shooting 1 of 6 from 3. Joel Embiid had 16 points and 6 rebounds while shooting 2 of 9 from the field.

The end result was a blowout win for the Celtics (9-2) to overtake the 76ers (9-3) for the best record in the Eastern Conference.

When it was over, Brown shared hugs with several of his former Celtics teammates. But he walked off the court without acknowledging Tatum as Tatum gave a postgame interview to NBC.

Tatum, meanwhile, didn't say Brown's name in his interview while downplaying the meaning of Tuesday's win.

"They all count as one," Tatum said of the game result. "No game is bigger than the other, definitely in the regular season. It's one game. It's one game. The hoopla is definitely over, and we get ready for tomorrow."

Considering the chatter leading up to Tuesday's game, Brown's cold reception to Tatum was expected.

Tatum has downplayed any friction with his former All-NBA teammate.

"There's no animosity, there's no beef," Tatum said previously when talking about his relationship with Brown.

For Brown, who was vocal about his multitude of grievances before the Celtics traded him in the offseason, there's clearly beef. Or lamb chops, as he prefers.

"There's no beef, but there might be a little lamb chops and gravy," Brown previously opined on his relationship with Tatum.

Brown doubled down on Sunday that he doesn't have anything to talk about with Tatum.

"I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said, per ESPN's Kris Rhim. "Just playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win, so nothing to talk about. Just check the ball up."

Check the ball up, they did — this time in favor of Tatum and the Celtics.

#2682. Oregon star edge rusher Teitum Tuioti out for the season

EUGENE — One of Oregon football's most important defensive players is done for the season.

Ducks senior defensive end Teitum Tuioti suffered a season-ending knee injury in Oregon's 41-28 win over Ohio State, Dan Lanning announced on Monday.

"Teitum has been unbelievable for us this year, and every year he's been here," Lanning said. "Just watching him grow as a player and person has been a lot of fun for us. But unfortunately Teitum's done for the year, he had a knee injury, he'll end up having surgery."

Tuioti was among the Ducks' leaders in tackles with 44, and ranked second on the team in sacks with 5.5 on the season. The former Sheldon High School star sits at No. 8 all-time for Oregon with 22.5 sacks across his four seasons, providing steady leadership on a talented and experienced defensive front.

In the win over the Buckeyes, he also showed off his arm: Tuioti completed a pass to fellow defensive end Matayo Uiagalelei on a memorable fake punt which shifted momentum in the game.

"I hate it for him, because (the injury) was a routine, weird play that it happened on," Lanning said. "He left it on the line there on the field, and I don't know if he'll get another chance to play as an Oregon football player, but whoever gets to have that guy on their team in the future is gonna be really, really lucky."

Should Tuioti forgo his fifth year of eligibility and enter the NFL Draft, he is a projected second- or third-round pick according to some mock drafts.

#2681. Packers Film Room: Packers defense picks off Drake Maye 3 times

The Green Bay Packers stomped the New England Patriots this past weekend. Jordan Love was dealing, but so was the Packers defense. They picked off Drake Maye three times, and they started quickly, intercepting his first pass of the game.

The Patriots come out in 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR), starting in a completely balanced, 2×2 look. They motion a TE under the formation before the snap. They run a playfake away from the motion, then Drake Maye [10] starts to boots away from the fake, ultimately pulling up deep on a half-boot look.

The Packers are showing a single-high safety (Xavier McKinney [29]) before the snap, and that holds after the snap. Per SumerSports, the Packers rotate their safeties after the snap on 39.6% of their snaps, the 4th highest in the league. This time they stay in that single-high look (looks like Cover 3).

The Patriots are running Kyle Williams [18] on a deep post from the left, then bringing Mack Hollins [13] on a deep crosser. Initially, it looks like McKinney is going to be running with Williams on the post, but, as Maye climbs in the pocket, McKinney breaks down on Hollins on the crosser.

The Packers have the second level of their defense dropped extremely deep, which makes the throw to Hollins a difficult one. Evan Williams [33] is sitting right under the place Maye wants to go. Maye climbs up in pocket, and it looks like he's doing that as a way to try to pull those defenders away from the window.

While Hollins is looking to settle into a window behind Williams, Maye throws across the field, where McKinney is waiting.

McKinney returns it 36 yards, setting up the Packers with 1st & 10 on the Patriots 14. They scored 2 plays later on a Jordan Love scramble to make it 7-0.

The Patriots are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) in a 3×1 formation. Kyle Williams is the lone receiver on the left. They've got a concept on the right that Maye can work, or he can take Williams on a vertical route if he likes that match-up.

The Packers are showing press coverage on the outside and their safeties are pulled up tight to the line. Evan Williams is the safety to the single receiver side. Just before the snap, he starts to bail to the middle. This looks like man-to-man coverage with the safety bailing away from the single WR side. That would put Kyle Williams man-to-man on Brandon Cisse [2] with no safety help, a match-up Maye clearly likes.

It's a really cool bit of deception from the Packers. Maye thinks he caught the Packers showing their hand a bit early, with Evan Williams bailing before the ball is snapped. Instead, it's the Packers showing Maye what he believes is a single-high rotation, but it quickly turns into a two-high look at the snap. Evan Williams goes from bailing to the middle to dropping wide as soon as the ball is snapped, with Javon Bullard [7] dropping to a deep zone on the other side of the field. Really subtle bit of deception here.

Maye has a bit of time so he ends up seeing that Evan Williams has dropped to a deep half-zone, but it's not a wide drop so Maye still thinks he can hit Kyle Williams.

As soon as Maye starts his throwing motion, Evan Williams looks like he's shot out of a cannon to the sideline. Cisse is in great position and he tips the ball to Evan Williams, who makes the pick.

It's impossible for me to see a tipped INT and not think of the classic Mike-McKenzine-to-Tyrone-Williams tip against the 49ers in the 2001 Wild Card Game.

Patriots are in 12 personnel in a shotgun, 3×1 formation. They are, once again, using Kyle Williams on a vertical route and bringing Eli Raridon [82] from the other side on a crossing route. To help spring that open, they've got Hunter Henry [85] on a curl route underneath. Push the defense vertical with Kyle Williams, pin down the second level with Henry and hit Raridon behind it. Nice idea.

Packers are starting with McKinney as the single-high safety, aligned extremely deep over the trips side. At the snap, he sinks down into a deep-half zone, with Evan Williams dropping into a deep-half zone on the other side. This looks like Cover 2, with Cisse passing off the vertical route from Kyle Williams to McKinney.

This should all work, but McKinney goes and makes a play. Maye hitches roughly a thousand times, looking to the route from Raridon in the middle. McKinney is still staying deep, but his hips are turned in and he's not even looking at the streaking Kyle Williams: he's looking to drive on Raridon.

As soon as Maye starts his throwing motion, McKinney triggers down, beating Raridon to the ball.

It was 17-7 at this point in the game. The Packers scored on a Kaleb Johnson rushing TD 3 plays later to take a 24-7 lead.

#2679. Jaylen Brown appears to blow off Jayson Tatum's greeting before Celtics-76ers

Their first interaction as opponents was very brief — if not entirely cold or indifferent.

In Philadelphia 76ers star Jaylen Brown's first game against the Boston Celtics, he seemingly ignored a quick greeting from former teammate Jayson Tatum, with whom he played for nine seasons.

The relationship between Brown and Tatum has cooled after the Celtics opted to move on from Brown, culminating in the July trade that sent Brown to the Sixers.

The two have talked publicly about their relationship and have indicated that they have not communicated since the deal.

During the moments right before tip-off Tuesday, Nov. 10, Tatum approached Brown and tapped Brown once on the right arm and twice on his chest as he walked past him. Brown, who was spinning the basketball on his finger, barely acknowledged Tatum and did not reciprocate the greeting.

As soon as the game tipped off, Brown was matched up guarding Tatum, and Tatum eventually forced Brown into a turnover on the other end when he swatted the ball off Brown's leg; there was significant contact on the play, but Tatum was not called for a foul.

Seconds later, after Brown had argued with officials, he committed a foul on Tatum.

After the game, which the Celtics won 123-101, Brown greeted many of his former teammates, but was not seen on the broadcast exchanging any pleasantries with Tatum.

#2677. It’s time to play the rookies

The Los Angeles Rams are down Puka Nacua, Davante Adams, Terrance Ferguson, and Jordan Whittington. Those were their top four receiving options atop the depth chart entering the year.

The NFL trade deadline passed and the Rams decided to stand pat. There are no reinforcements on the way.

They now will be left with Tutu Atwell, Konata Mumpfield, Colby Ferguson, Tyler Higbee, Xavier Smith, Brennen Presley, Davis Allen, and Max Klare.

CJ Daniels could shake up Rams receiving depth

Max Klare: Sean McVay gets his Dalton Kincaid years later

LA's passing game hasn't worked for most of this year. The offense will now need to right the ship with an unknown cast. A strong running game and an aggressive defense can only take you so far. The Rams have an incredibly thin margin for error for at least the next few games.

That probably gets the job done against the Arizona Cardinals and rookie quarterback Carson Beck. It will be an uphill battle in the games that follow versus the Green Bay Packers, Kansas City Chiefs, and San Francisco 49ers.

The main problem is that we've seen Atwell, Mumpfield, Parkinson, and Higbee for most of this year. None of them have been good enough. They aren't the answer moving forward.

Even if it's different for the sake of change. It's hard to be worse than Atwell and Mumpfield. If CJ Daniels cannot make an impact, then the Rams are already toast against stiffer competition.

The same goes for tight end Max Klare. LA drafted him in the second round. A redshirt year sounds ideal in a vacuum. The Rams no longer have the luxury of keeping him on the sidelines. He might have the most natural talent of any pass catcher left on the roster.

The Rams' approach of leading with patience has led to great results for player development. This time is different. LA has loaded its roster with superstars in hopes of winning a Super Bowl. They need to survive for at least the next three weeks.

Asking Daniels and Klare to be the difference may be an impossible task. They might be the only ones even remotely up to the challenge.

#2676. Damian Lillard is back and Ja Morant is here. How exactly is this going to work? | Bill Oram

In the history of basketball, we have certainly seen some why-would-they-do-that? pairings.

Jerseys and sleeves. Kawhi Leonard and a tree sponsorship. Utah and "the Jazz."

Once, there was even Detlef Schrempf and a headband, if you can believe that.

We're about to find out if they belong on such a list.

Because of all the things you might have said the Trail Blazers needed as they prepared to welcome Lillard back after making a playoff run without him, a slight-of-stature ball-dominant guard with a questionable jump shot would not have topped anyone's list.

Depth on the wing? Yes. Shooting? Definitely. Defense? Always.

Morant doesn't particularly address any of those, and yet, he's here, a dynamic two-time All-Star in need of a second act, being paid a team-high $42.1 million to play the same position as not just Lillard, but Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson.

Heck, the Blazers' most valuable point guard last season was forward Deni Avdija.

"I'm sure there will be questions about fit," General Manager Joe Cronin said Monday.

The Blazers have little more than three weeks before the regular season begins in which to figure that out. At the team's annual media day on Monday, Morant appeared in a fresh white No. 1 Trail Blazers jersey. It's happening.

"It's easy for people to be like, 'Man how is this going to work,'" Lillard offered. "'They can't do this, they can't do that.' But being on the floor with them … we can be a dangerous team and I really believe that."

The onus is on the Trail Blazers starting this month to prove that they bet right in acquiring Morant. And that pairing him with Lillard isn't the boondoggle conventional wisdom suggests it will be.

Lillard noted how many teams that succeeded in the playoffs last year, think San Antonio with its four point guards, relied on numerous playmakers. To his credit, Morant said he would be comfortable coming off the bench, if necessary.

But they would not be the first NBA team to fall into the trap of believing they are capable of adjusting or that they will be comfortable sacrificing. It isn't uncommon to see players in those situations default to familiar habits and sensibilities once the season is underway or struggles come.

That's what made a lot of the positive energy around what sure seems like an awkward roster ring so hollow. We're going to need to see it to believe it.

Morant tried to lay out a vision for how it could look. If he drives to the paint and is double-teamed, someone else is inevitably open. That's how basketball works.

"That allows me to have more space to be the best Ja I can be," Morant said.

The 36-year-old Holiday, who would be a more natural complement next to Lillard or Morant than they are to each other, made his own case for why the point guard rotation makes sense.

"It's about being a complete basketball player for myself," he said, "and I think we have a lot of guys like that."

There is a long history of teams talking themselves into superstar additions that make little sense. The Los Angeles Lakers once made a conscious decision to acquire Russell Westbrook and pair him with LeBron James. Nobody made them do that!

The talent and star power of a Lillard-Morant backcourt is undeniable. Still, I remain unconvinced that Cronin, with a very hands-on new owner in his ear, made the deal with winning basketball games at the front of mind.

Although, admittedly, Cronin's biggest wins as a GM have been in the trade market.

The haul of assets he collected for Lillard, only to get him back two years later, will go down as an all-time great swindle. So, too, will the oft-questioned Avdija trade a year later.

Maybe he sees something in a Lillard-Morant pairing that many of us can't.

Morant could return to the All-Star form he had achieved before injuries and off-court issues derailed his ascent. And if he does, the Blazers can either trade him for pieces that fit better or clear out the logjam and build around him.

But to sell the current roster as a basketball strategy doesn't quite pass the smell test.

Neither Lillard nor Morant has achieved stardom due to his defensive acumen. Each player needs the ball in his hands to thrive. If the duo is on the floor together, Avdija is no longer the secondary playmaker, he becomes tertiary.

So, you are left to wonder whether the Blazers sold themselves on Morant because of how he can help the current collection of talent or if they simply saw the opportunity to land a 27-year-old All-NBA talent for cheap, regardless of what it meant for the existing roster construction.

And if you're being honest, you probably don't need to wonder which of the two it is.

"We were very focused and we'll continue to be on … adding to our talent base as much as we can," Cronin said.

That thinking right there may tell you just how far ahead of everyone else the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder are in the Western Conference. They are positioned to dominate for the next half-decade, if not longer. The only chance any other team has of disrupting that is taking bold risks.

But I thought the goal was to go all in on the twilight years of Lillard's career?

"Dame literally just wants to win," said first-year head coach Micah Nori, whose charge is to sort out arguably the most talented glut of point guard talent in NBA history. "I think that's the only thing left he really has to (do). He's already proven he's a winner, but at the highest level."

Does adding Morant move Lillard closer to a title? Or simply give Portland a potential off-ramp if Lillard is no longer the same player after tearing his Achilles tendon?

Morant was without question a low-risk, high-reward addition. He came at the reasonable price of Jerami Grant and Kris Murray. If it becomes clear that Morant is one point guard too many, or that he's just not the player he once was, some will argue that it didn't cost the Blazers much to try.

However, there is an opportunity cost to messing with Lillard's swan song. If you don't get it right, you risk wasting the gift of his voluntary return last summer. And, not for nothing, Lillard has the option to become a free agent again after this season.

The franchise icon certainly hasn't said anything that would suggest he is unhappy about Morant's presence, although he stopped short on Monday of a full-throated endorsement. He said he knew about the trade before it went through.

When I asked if he thought it was a good idea right away or if he needed time to get on board with the plan, Lillard said, "My position on it was, I'm prepared for whatever."

It's good that he's already thinking about other positions. Because his old one is getting awfully crowded.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

Embiid's health has been a career-long issue for him, and the Sixers have declined to play him in back-to-back games. #2671. Despite hurt wrist, Antetokounmpo scores 30 and Heat outlast Jazz 115-109

SALT LAKE CITY (AP) — Giannis Antetokounmpo scored 30 points, Davion Mitchell added 19 points, and the Miami Heat outlasted the depleted Utah Jazz 115-109 on Tuesday night.

The Heat also got 14 from Pelle Larsson but needed late blocks from Klay Thompson and Bam Adebayo to secure their third win in their last four games.

Antetokounmpo iced his sprained right wrist in a heavy wrap when he was on the bench but it didn't seem to bother him on the court. He shot 12 for 21 and grabbed 11 rebounds.

He now has 21,836 points and passed Gary Payton to become the 39th leading scorer in NBA history.

Despite the Jazz's ninth straight loss, Utah's two teenagers gave the Jazz hope for the future. Rookie Darryn Peterson nearly set his career high (26) for the second game in a row with 25 points and Ace Bailey scored 23.

Utah's Isaiah Collier, a notoriously poor shooter who had not made a 3-pointer this season, made four consecutive shots from behind the arc in the fourth quarter to cut Miami's lead to 101-93.

Then Svi Mykhailiuk made back-to-back baskets to cut the lead to 112-107 in the final minute but it was too late for the Jazz, who were missing four starters to injury — Lauri Markkanen (wrist), Keyonte George (ankle), Jaren Jackson Jr. (knee), and Jusuf Nurkic (foot).

Antetokounmpo's shooting sparked the Heat to a 15-2 run in the third quarter to give the Heat the cushion they needed and send them home with a 3-2 record on their five-game road trip.

Larsson hit a 3-pointer with 6:58 left in the second quarter to cap a 13-1 run and make it 49-32 for Miami.

The Jazz, who have been hurt by turnovers all season, had 18 to just eight for the Heat.

Heat: Host Cleveland on Friday night to commence a five-game homestand.

Jazz: Host Orlando on Wednesday to complete the back-to-back set.

The Wolverines didn't score until late in the game, and the following day, head coach Kyle Whittingham fired offensive coordinator Jason Beck.

Things bottomed out so bad for the Wolverines against the injury-depleted Spartans, Michigan's football team actually got a mention in the Nov. 7 incident report from the City of Ann Arbor Fire Department posted on Facebook. Of the 90 calls for service, one actually reported an "offensive line figurative Dumpster fire at Michigan Stadium."

Must be something in the water in Washtenaw County (where they actually did have a literal pissing contest Saturday). Eastern Michigan lost to Central Michigan, 35-7, at Ford Field in Detroit on Wednesday, Nov. 4. In that game, the Eagles didn't get a first down until late in the first half, and they also didn't score until late in the game.

Of the state's five football teams, only Western Michigan has sealed a bowl game (six wins). No coincidence, Western Michigan also is the only one of the five teams with stability at the quarterback position. The other teams have made changes, either related to injury or poor performance.

#2664. NBA Panic Meter: Why Nuggets, Heat, Suns should be worried after just two weeks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We've now seen two weeks of the 2026-27 season. Is that enough time to draw conclusions? Almost certainly not. No team has even played 10% of its schedule yet, and outlier stretches are inevitable. Case in point: last year's champion, the New York Knicks, had a mostly healthy 2-9 stretch last January that included losses to the tanking Dallas Mavericks and Sacramento Kings. Weird things can happen for a few weeks.

But the first few weeks give us our first taste of who these teams are, and inevitably several will be worse than we expected. We may not have seen enough of a sample at this point to write anyone off completely, but alarm bells are starting to ring in a few notable markets. So let's go through a few of these struggling teams and figure out just how much reason there is to panic after two weeks.

It's easy to forget this now, but New York's championship season started relatively slowly. The Knicks won their first two games, but lost their next three. Mike Brown gave a lengthy and informative monologue about some of their process issues after one of those losses, a road defeat at the hands of the Milwaukee Bucks, and the Knicks righted the ship from there. And aside from that disastrous January stretch, they were mostly great.

It's hard not to look back on that stretch now, as the Knicks limp through a slow start to their title defense. Brown has echoed many of the same criticisms he made last October, most notably the offense's tendency to stand around rather than committing to the all-out motion machine that powered the greatest playoff offense of all time last spring. Perhaps that style wasn't fully replicable for this group across 82 games. That doesn't mean it can't be summoned again in April. All four Knicks losses have come by single digits. I'm going to need more than two weeks before I start worrying about Jalen Brunson's team in clutch settings. The Knicks were the fourth-most efficient late-clock shooting team in the NBA this season. They're 28th so far this season. That's going to change.

Brunson's offseason wrist surgery is a reasonable concern. His shooting is down from everywhere, even the foul line. Maybe he'll need a midseason break to get right. Mikal Bridges is (slowly) starting to make shots again. He needs to be more aggressive, and his on-ball defense has slipped. He was never going to match the intensity he played with in the postseason given his aversion to contact, but he'll have to improve on this front. Karl-Anthony Towns needs to stop fouling, but that's hardly new. Josh Hart is missing too much in the paint, but it's too early to draw conclusions there. OG Anunoby will start making 3s because he always does.

The October Knicks look like a team that spent July, August and September celebrating. If they still look like that in December, panic becomes reasonable. For now, the concerns are relatively light. They have a proven formula, and the big concern that did exist before the season -- the backup center situation -- has thus far been a relative strength. A championship earns you quite a bit more grace than the rest of these teams deserve.

If you shouldn't write off teams after two weeks, then you certainly shouldn't do so to rookies. Still, Darryn Peterson has certainly been the worst of the much-ballyhooed top four in June's draft. He's never getting to the basket or the line, not quite prerequisites for stardom at his size given his shooting, but enormously important traits for an aspiring star guard. Defense has been an adventure as well, though that's to be expected for a rookie guard, and the early returns on his fit with Keyonte George have been clunky. The Jazz ranking 29th in offense for any stretch in which they're actively trying to win is jarring. Will Hardy had the Jazz in the top five offensively in his debut 2022-23 season before the front office broke up the team at the trade deadline.

One of the motivating factors in selecting Peterson over Rookie of the Year favorite Cameron Boozer was February's acquisition of Jaren Jackson Jr., who is currently sidelined with a torn MCL. Considering his injury history in Memphis, his long-term reliability poses real concerns, yet Utah banked most of its interior defense on him, at least in the short term, when it traded Walker Kessler to the Lakers. It's hard not to wonder about an alternate timeline in which the Jazz chose Boozer and kept Kessler instead of trading for Jackson.

If we were purely talking about the 2026-27 season, the panic meter would be higher here. We're not. The Jazz wanted to be competitive this season. There's still plenty of time for that to happen, and the eventual return of Jusuf Nurkić should help on that front for a Utah team that has gotten very little out of the center position. The real championship window, even under the most optimistic projections, was always a few years down the line. The Jazz are still young and asset-rich. There's plenty of time to right the ship. Teams with more invested in this season specifically can't say the same.

The defense is bad, but the defense is always bad. They're at the bottom of the league in 3-point volume, but they're always at the bottom of the league in 3-point volume. Aaron Gordon is no longer finding easy looks at the rim nor finishing remotely effectively, but he's spent most of the last two seasons hurt, so he might simply need time to work himself back into a groove. These were predictable concerns. Nikola Jokić was supposed to paper over them like he always does.

So far this year, he hasn't. The best player of the 2020s is suddenly human, and the Nuggets are not built to win with Jokić as anything less than divine. His own defense has been perpetually shaky, but he's always at least been an elite possession-finisher. Since becoming a full-time starter in his second season, he's never had a defensive rebounding rate below 26%. He's below 22% so far this season. He's currently tying his career-high in turnovers per game, and his assists are back to single digits for the first time since 2024.

The real issues, though, are with his scoring. Jokić's overall statistical decline after a midseason knee injury last season was well documented, but what flew under the radar at the time was the precipitous decline in his 3-point shooting following a wrist injury. This was a big driver of last season's playoff upset at the hands of the Minnesota Timberwolves. Rudy Gobert didn't have to defend him out to the 3-point line, and considering Denver's shooting deficiencies elsewhere, that allowed the Wolves to completely take away the rim. Jokić is 7-of-31 from 3 so far this season. More distressingly, his legendary intermediate finishing is slipping. After five straight years in the 95th percentile or better in terms of efficiency, his runner is down to the 86th percentile, according to Synergy Sports. His hook shot, similarly dominant, is in the 50th. His free-throw attempt rate has nearly been cut in half since last season.

There's no point in talking about the defense, the shooting, or the iffy DeMar DeRozan fit if this is the case. Either Jokić is one of the best two or three players in the world or the Nuggets are not to be taken seriously as a championship contender. Jokić has earned a lot more deference than a six-game judgment. Nobody should be surprised if he's the MVP frontrunner in a month. Those other concerns will merit closer looks if he is, because even the idealized version of this roster is pretty flawed. But there's no scenario in which these Nuggets meaningfully contend if Jokić doesn't improve. For now, that's really all that matters here.

The Suns earn the dubious distinction of becoming the first team of the 2026-27 season to have their dysfunction leaked to the press. Ironically, the thing they're reportedly upset about isn't even really the problem. Chris Haynes has reported that the Suns locker room is frustrated by the roster's lack of a point guard. But Phoenix does have a point guard; it just isn't starting him. Let's compare Phoenix's offense with Collin Gillespie on the floor to how it plays without him, using stats from Cleaning the Glass.

This isn't rocket science. The Suns assist on almost 74% of their made field goals when Gillespie plays and below 60% when he doesn't. Both Devin Booker and Miles Bridges see their true shooting improve by at least eight percentage points with Gillespie on the floor. Starting Jalen Green isn't working. Whether it's in deference to his status as a No. 2 overall pick, his contract or an unfounded belief in his value, this experiment has failed. It's time to start Gillespie and add a more traditional point guard behind him.

So the point guard issues are solvable. You know what the bigger problem is? The Suns have completely lost the high-effort identity they built last season. Let's compare where the Suns ranked last year and this year in some notable areas.

Some of this comes down to bad opponents' shooting luck. Some of it is the absence of Mark Williams, because it has forced Khaman Maluach into a role he simply is not ready for (center has been perhaps Phoenix's biggest problem area). Most of it is rotational. Green isn't exactly known for playing hard or defending. Neither is Miles Bridges. Key players from last year like Jordan Goodwin, Ryan Dunn and Rasheer Fleming are playing less. The Suns simply aren't talented enough to win at the rate they did last year if they aren't playing as hard as they did then.

The Suns don't exactly have a pivot here. They don't control any of their own first-round picks in the seven-year trade window except for a 2032 selection that is currently frozen. They're not going to be able to trade Booker for a haul and reboot this thing, either. He's 30, never gets to the rim and is a declining 3-point shooter who seemingly needs to play next to the right type of playmaking point guard. His supermax contract has albatross potential. After giving up their 2033 first-round pick for Bridges, the Suns largely locked themselves into this core for the foreseeable future. There was never championship upside here, but for a team this heavily leveraged, this level of performance is simply unacceptable.

The following clip sums up one of Miami's biggest ongoing challenges:

Look at Tim Hardway here.. and then look at davion pic.twitter.com/qPTTtlY0Oq

The Heat have a reputation, and one of its pillars is defensive tenacity. Davion Mitchell obviously has that in spades. But given the unorthodox roster-building challenges of using two big men as your primary shot creators, the Heat have had to embrace players that don't. Tim Hardaway Jr. is on this roster because the Heat so badly need shooting around Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. He is not yet making shots. He is also doing, well, this, defensively. Klay Thompson is getting hunted more mercilessly than almost any player in the NBA. The Heat have shooting. They have defense. They have alarmingly few players who offer both.

They have even fewer who can create their own shots. Antetokounmpo, Adebayo and Mitchell are the only members of the Heat who generated at least 30% of their made field goals without an assist. Toss Andrew Wiggins onto the pile, and everyone else who averages at least 10 minutes a game is assisted on 80% or more of their made shots.

Wiggins is averaging career-lows in everything. Miami's relatively egalitarian, pick-and-roll-less offense of a season ago suited him. Adjusting to the Antetokounmpo show thus far has been a struggle. Nikola Jović is veering dangerously close to dead money on their cap for the next four years. None of the core players, not Mitchell, nor Antetokounmpo, nor even Adebayo, is defending at the level expected. This was supposed to be a top-five defense. It's been in the bottom five thus far, and while some opponent shooting regression is coming, Miami's defense is designed to allow the very 3-pointers that are killing it.

Aside from simply having one of the best players in the world, it's hard to point to a distinct strength for the Heat. They're not shooting, defending or rebounding especially well. They're not winning the possession game. They're running quite a bit, but their transition offense ranks 24th in efficiency, according to Synergy Sports.

This is a team very much still finding itself, but it's one without many of the tools that made Antetokounmpo's Milwaukee teams work or the distinct advantages Miami's vaunted culture typically created for it. This roster is at least a trade or two away, but with minimal draft capital, addressing the holes here will be difficult. It might take multiple transaction cycles to get this right.

Antetokounmpo is in his 30s now and has a growing history of lower-body injuries. He might not have that many more prime seasons to waste. He's playing at a superstar level right now, and it just isn't clear how equipped Miami is to take advantage of that after giving up practically everything of value it had besides Adebayo just to get him.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.
